whetted the appetite of the leaders of nullification
to renew the contest for the black line
across the continent, which they have always
looked to as opening the whole of Mexico to
spoliation; to become at last a vast addition to
the empire of slave states.

We have labored through this tissue of insidious legislation, to fix the public mind on
one important point. It is, that while pretending to make the compromise of 1850 the foundation of their legislation, they actually repealed it. They falsely assume that the compromise of 1850 repealed the prohibition of
slavery in New Mexico; they convert into a
declaratory act what they call the non-intervention principle, giving the territorial settlers
in New Mexico, the right to establish slavery
there. When as law stood before, slavery
was excluded by the paramount law of the
mother country, which law continued after its
annexation to ours, and until repealed by the
Nebraska act.

This new attempt the authors well knew
was built on double falsehood. They knew
that "the principle of non-intervention by Congress with slavery, in the territories" so far
from being recognised by any legislation of
Congress, was in fact refuted by its uninterrupted legislation on the subject of slavery,
from the foundation of the government. They
knew that the compromise of 1850 recognized
the right of Mexico, in like manner, to exclude
slavery from its province of New Mexico, and
that the law of nations brought it under our
jurisdiction, with its local laws and customs
and domestic institutions unrepealed, as was
the case with the Illinois territory, when required.

They recoil from the agitation of slavery.
Well, what has occasioned this agitation?
Was not the whole country quieted by the compromises of 1850 and 1854? Did not the
national conventions of both parties accede to
these settlements, and did not the President
elected by the victorious party, give in his adhesion, both before and after his election, and
pledge the power he had just assumed, when
he took the oath of office, to the preservation
of the peace agreed on between the north and
south? And, in utter contempt of all these
vows, both by parties in the south and all the
Douglasites—the followers of the President in
the north, led on by him, have conspired to
overthrow the pacification, and the country
is thrown into commotions.

These extracts are taken from an article denouncing the course of Douglas and Atkinson
in the repeal of the Compromise, and exposing their bad faith and falseness.

A horrible tragedy occurred at Bergholtz,
German settlement in the town of Wheatland in
this county, on Saturday night last, being nothing
less than the cold blooded butchery of Dr. T. A.
Strange, his housekeeper and daughter, by some
person or persons as yet unknown.

Sunday morning, one of the doctor's neighbors was proceeding along the road leading from
the doctor's house South, he came upon the lifeless
body lying in the road, with pool of blood
by its side. He had been murdered with an
axe, having been struck four blows with it, one
on the right side of the face, two upon the back
of the head, and one upon the right side. The mur-
derer evidently meant to make sure work; either
blow would have killed the victim. On proceeding
to the house a mile distant, still more horrible
sight presented itself.

Upon the floor was the bleeding corpse of Mrs.
Barlean, the housekeeper of Dr. Strange, her
head having been literally cut in two by the same
instrument which had caused the death of the doc-
tor, and a short distance from her, upon the bed
was found the lifeless remains of the young daugh-
ter of Dr. Strange. The girl like the others had
been killed by an axe. The first blow had been
given on the side of the face, and before the sec-
ond, the victim had raised the arm in self defence
and received the second blow upon the elbow and
fleshy part of the arm. The first blow must have
caused almost instant death.

So far, not the slightest clue to the perpetrator
of this horrible deed or the cause which led to it,
had been detected. A neighbor of Dr. Strange who
lives nearby, was up all Saturday night finishing
a pair of boots which he had promised, but said he
heard nothing to excite his attention. The gen-
eral impression is that the person or persons who
committed the murder went to the house and called
the doctor away on business. He had a large
overcoat on, and a lantern which he always carried
when going out at nights, which was found near
where his body lay.

It is supposed that after murdering the doctor,
the assassin went back and murdered the woman
and child to prevent detection. Mrs. Barlean when
found, had a candle in one hand and matches in
the other, and was probably about to make a light
when she was struck a deadly blow. Dr. Strange
had been in this country about six years and has
resided all this time at Bergholtz. He separated
from his wife about two years ago, since which she
has lived at Buffalo.

Mrs. Barlean is a woman about 30 years old, and
has kept house for Dr. Strange since his wife left. She
has a husband in Germany who she was expecting
here daily. The other victim was Dr. Strange's
daughter, a beautiful young girl about 10 years
old. Amid the speculations which such a startling
tragedy always gives rise to, the only one which has
pretended to give any solution of the crime is this:
There has been a hoop maker living near Bergholtz,
for whom the doctor has practiced a good deal; and
who owed him quite a large bill. Frequent quar-
rels have risen out of this fact. This man moved
to Buffalo a short time ago, however, and there is
no direct testimony that he has been about Ber-
gholtz lately.

The Coroner's investigation which is now in pro-
gress, it is to be hoped will elicit something which
will lead to the detection of the person or persons
guilty of this most diabolical deed, which, for its
brutal atrocity has scarce a parallel. Neither sex
nor age, innocence nor beauty was any barrier to
the consummation of the fiendish purpose which
led to the committal of this triple murder.

BY E. W. Brown, which was destroyed

In his address to his reader, Mr. Brown
says:

to offer anything like full reply to the views of the gen

opinion as to the purport of past legislation and as to the

claiming these for authority to sustain their own respec

now, hardly probable that discussion of these points
this time will do any towards adjusting them.
We cannot know what has been the purport of that
legislation, to what Washington or Jefferson would
do if called to heal present dissensions, and hence pre-
fer to pass all such questions and to go at once to deal
with facts, opinions, prejudices, passions, and all this com
plex web of difficulties that actually exist shaking and
distracting the country.


Primarily the difference between those who are in
controversy upon the slavery question is to be found in their
conflicting views of the nature, justice and propriety of
slavery itself. Northern belief holds it to be an evil and
curse, while in the South it is regarded no offence
against either the laws of God or humanity; and since discussion has been forced upon the subject, they have been
driven to examine it, only connected with the social
and economical interests of the white in regions
where slavery most naturally thrives; but in the light of
facts which show the real condition of the negro in the
southern mind (more of late years than before) is
actually adopting the conclusion that the institution is a
positive good. Thus radically opposed in opinion, and there
being likelihood that they will agree or the more
this subject is discussed and debated, especially under the
prejudices and passions which in large portions of
the people of both sides, the wider the separation
of their minds will grow—what is to be done to prevent that u

and the other right? Consider the condition into which
this controversy is brought, and think; gentlemen will be

the constitution for something pertaining to the issue thus

in regard to it, we will look in vain. The express words

it is hoped, that it would be decided in the
spirit of justice, equality, and forbearing patriotism, such
as the constitution had brought forth and flushed the constitution itself.

nothing in the constitution to forbid the equal enjoyment
of common territory by all citizens of the United States.

gentlemen who are adverse to the institution of slavery.

interests and all conflicting views of policy; and, also, that

even incidentally against that interest to be unwarranted

the constitution recognizes secures and protects men who owe
fealty to it? Should it not barishly condemn or rudely touch it?


If we would determine alright between these parties, we
must look to their positions and claims they present.

We have no doubt it would be gratifying to DR. Stribling's numerous friends, and to the friends of the Asylum, generally, if he would reconsider his determination to retire from the position he has so long occupied and in which he has been so eminently useful. Such, at least, we believe is the feeling in this community.

To the Editor of the Indicator.

SIR—I find in the advertisement of Mr. Niche, President of the Board of Visitors, of the Western Lunatic Asylum, contained in the last issue of your paper, confirmation of the news that DR. L. L. Stribling has resigned the position of Superintendent, which he has held for many years, and in which he has effected so much good and achieved such an enviable and widespread reputation; and avail myself of the occasion to make a few suggestions to the Board, which I trust they will believe proceeds from no impertinent disposition on my part to interfere with the discharge of their official duties, but solely from the interest I feel in great public charity, no doubt in common with a large majority of the community.

It is, I believe, generally conceded in this community, where Dr. S. is known, and in which the results of his treatment of the insane have been more particularly observed, that he possesses rare qualities for the discharge of the duties of his station. These qualities are of a two-fold nature, and are seldom found united in the same person, comprehending professional learning and ability, and practical acquaintance with the forms of business, with capacity for administration. The most inexperienced can see at a glance what difficulties surround the head of an establishment containing, probably, NOT far from 600 persons, consisting of Assistant Physicians, Ward Keepers, Stewards, Waiters, Laundresses, Gardeners, Engineers, Laborers, &C., and something over 400 insane, nearly moiety of whom are females, and each one requiring a different or at least modified form of medical treatment. It is useless, therefore, to dilate on this subject. All agree that it requires high qualities, hard to be found in one man; and the question then occurs, what are the prospects of the Board for procuring such a successor to DR. S.? I hazard nothing in saying that they are slim; though there is much professional and administrative ability in the State, unfortunately they are not united.

I therefore think the causes ought to be ascertained, such course is not disagreeable to Dr. S., which induced him to sever his connection with the institution, and that the Board should remove them if possible. Possibly DR. S. has been saddled with more labor than is proper, and agreeable to him, or possible to be performed. IF SO, his labors should be lightened. I understand that among his numerous duties he is required to audit all the accounts of the institution. This is wrong. A clerk should attend to this important minutia. Possibly his salary is too small—and this I believe. SINCE it was raised to its present figure the expenses of living have been greatly increased, and what was then a fair compensation is now wholly inadequate. But I will not undertake to discuss this matter, as all of the considerations I could suggest will no doubt occur to the Board. I make these remarks because I believe the public interest would be greatly advanced by retaining DR. S. in his present position, and with no "ulterior designs." They may go for what they are worth. And I wish it understood that I make them without the knowledge of DR. S., or any member of his family, or indeed any connection of his, and are simply the views of a gentleman in no wise connected by blood or marriage with him or his family, in no way connected with the Hospital, but merely and independent and unpretending.

FARMER.

Correspondence Of the Missouri Democrat.

KANSAS, Dec. 9, 1855.—Since my last, everything here has been in a great state of excitement; the news brought during the last twenty-four hours has greatly changed the aspect of affairs. Yesterday, at 10 o'clock, was the hour mentioned for the attack to commence, but by some means it did not.

The last news was brought to us last night about 10 o'clock, by parties who left here on Wednesday morning last, and have been at Lawrence all the time. From their report it appears that Gov. Shannon has stepped out of his former position, and declares he has been imposed upon and misinformed as to the true state of things. He finds that his informants are men interested in having Lawrence destroyed, as they are all pro-slavery men, and interested in the town of Lecompton, and Lawrence is, of course, a great bugbear to them.

The Missourian men numbered about 1900 men in both camps. At Lawrence they had collected about 200 men, who came there to die or be victorious. They were fighting for their homes and families, while the mob on the other hand, had nothing at stake but the pleasing of a few political hacks. After Gov. Shannon had a conversation with some of the men from Lawrence, he saw his folly, and the entire strength of Lawrence placed itself in his hands for the preservation of the public peace, and the sustaining of all constitutional laws. So that, he had to accept them, and by that means they have disarmed the mob party.

And now that the mob and they have been thereupon, the representatives of the nation, if a few interested men, they are loud in their denunciation of them, and wouldn't mind fighting among themselves. I have been talking with men who have just come in from the scene, and they say the Missourians are leaving for their respective homes, as fast as they can, and they seem to be of one mind. Damn Kansans, they may go to hell before they come over again. This is the third time they have come clear out the darned "Yankees," and each time have gone home without a fight, and they are now convinced that the men they have to deal with are not made of straw.

I know of some instances of personal exposure, that are truly beautiful to contemplate. the migration of free negroes to
their limits. If they find this desirable
now, what measures would they not take
to secure the same end in case the South
should emancipate all her slaves? Why,
if necessary, the borders of the Northern
States would be lined with police and
forts to keep back the three and a half
millions of emancipated slaves in the
South. Well, here they would be among
us. Nature has stamped them as an inferior race of human beings. A man
who, in this day of scientific advance as
well as practical observation, doubts this
is a fool. They are, BY nature, lazy and
improvident and utterly careless. Hence
from their destitute condition and unappre-
ciative as they would be of labor, time, money, as of everything else, the

price of labor would almost at once be re-
duced to a minimum that would keep
body and soul together. This, of course,
would drag the white laborer down to
the same wretched pittance and reduce
him to the same degraded condition and
level. In the mean time the wealthy class
of Southern society would suffer but little
in this way. Wealth can always create
an artificial position that will preserve
its possessors from social degradation.
Besides, the wealthy land holders could
emigrate if they so desired, and perhaps
living in luxurious ease, amid the aristo-
cratic circles of London or Paris,
could draw their QUARTERLY rents from
America, while the poor white man
would be struggling with the free negro
for a crust of bread, upon the soil where
his fathers died in prosperity and plenty.
Indeed, we hold that should the slave
holders themselves ever become so de-
termined as to seek to effect the abolition
of slavery, the white laboring class in
the South should rise up in body against it; and we much mistake their in-
telligence and spirit if they would not do it.

How it has frightened the face of Thompson, our landlord, with his four hundred souls to provide for, big and little; for Thompson well knows that green corn, sweet potatoes, bread and butter, beefsteaks, and even Shrewsbury oystercakes, depend upon timely and liberal rains.

The weather now is fine, elastic and exhilarating. There is glorious surf over the bar, cool, calm, salt water river at our feet, and romantic hills and valleys and watery expanses and green Islands around the corner of Rocky Point; and now is the time, N. B., to finish the visit which you commenced while yet the heated term, the south winds, and the mosquitoes combined to spoil our pleasures.

Pleasures. We know that the carping Roundhead with his folly—"twenty-six what pleasure is in the crowd of watering place hotel, with its dressing and fussing and endless outings and dissipations." What pleasure in the miscellaneous multitude about you, and in the noise and confusion that reign paramount in the scramble for dinner, in the silly hottentots all around the house, and in the loss of rest by day and of sleep by night, from the endless middling scraping, dancing, singing young ladies', noisy wants and squalling children. These questions are natural to crusty, crabbed, dyspeptical old bachelors, who prefer to be alone. But very tiresome notion of our fellow citizens of the regular sort people who love society, old and young, and who actually enjoy themselves at just such places as this; and get strong and fat upon good feeding, good air, good wholesome food &c. among the hills, among the waves, eligible from business, and the cultivation of an amiable disposition. It is change from the dull monotones of every day life, and we have great safety. Of people around us much the better, the society anywhere would be exceedingly fat and stupid if we were all exactly alike.

Our NJ tourists, who would run away from the vanities of Watering place, have their substitutes in their camp meetings. They assemble in the woods by thousands, they sleep in tents, they are drenched in the rains, they live upon the coarsest fare for days together, they deny themselves in these to unions, most of the solid comforts of homeland. What for? Some may cry for the sake of revival religion; but it is all much, too easily, for the novelties of the thing, for social attractions and an agreeable change from the dull routine of every day life. So it is with us here. Away with your carping philosophy. Let that man pass who pulls up his rose—handsome woman who has one dress for breakfast, another for the bath, another for the morning ride, another for dinner, another for the afternoon sail, another for tea, and another for the evening hop. Suppose she has—suppose she does. We ask, does she not give employment to dressmakers, and will not the dry goods man attest that these things are the secres of our great commercial prosperity? Talk of the follies, foppery, summeries and nonsense of the watering places as much as you please, father Puritan, there is much of good sound philosophy in them after all. Reason in all things—oh yes, but your spendthrift keeps money in circulation, and does good, while your miser is a drone in the hive.

Look at our sensible old men here, our sensible and excellent mothers with their children, our young ladies, blondes and brunettes, our young bachelors, and take the vote upon it, in a month on the seaside at Cape May, NJ, Newport, Nahant, the Repose, Rockaway, Bath, or, who're with mountains and sea combined, here, at Thompson's, for instance. Ask them, we say. It is months relaxation, fun and folly as such a place, is not a good thing for a night, or even a week or a day or a night. Look at those who have been here the longest, and see if they are not the strongest. Ask the first lady you meet—ask Thompson—ask the doctor.

the New York Commissioners of Immigration for
the year 1855 contains some statements of gene-
ral interest. From it we learn that during that
period no less than 1885 destitute and diseas-
ed alien immigrants were relieved, forwarded
and provided with employment by the Commis-
sioners. This is more than the whole number
of immigrant arrivals at that port during the year,

years, though the far greater part had found oc-

LEAVENWORTH JOURNAL,

ABOUT THE FIRST OF JUNE.

1st. We are induced to engage in this endeavor from conviction that another paper is required by the growing population of Kansas, and the public demand for full and reliable information in regard to its history, topography, climate, soil, resources, politics, present condition and future prospects. Such information we can readily furnish here, since Leavenworth is the commercial metropolis of the Territory—occupying a position of direct intercourse with two thirds of its population, and is the focus of news.

2d. We believe that the institution of Black Slavery is a moral, political and economical blessing—that it is right in principle and expedient in policy, and hence should be defended and extended. It is our purpose to maintain these propositions in our paper, and do all in our power to make Kansas a slave State. In the discussion of the slavery question, however, we will never deviate to maintain a conservative position, to present arguments and facts instead of denunciation and abuse.

3d. Although the Leavenworth Journal will be devoted to Politics in great degree, yet it will pay due regard to the Good, the True and the Beautiful. It will exhibit a faithful portraiture of the times in which we live, by presenting a correct account of the current events of the day, the progress of the Arts and Sciences, of Education, Commerce, Agriculture and Internal Improvements. It will discuss all subjects with freedom and firmness; give all parties their dues, and follow the light of truth.

If our Weekly Journal meets with cordial support, we intend soon to publish a Semi-Weekly and perhaps a Daily.
